explanation: Vitamin C in bell pepper can help the body absorb non-heme iron from lentils. Compounds in tea may have the opposite effect when the drink accompanies the meal. Keeping the pepper and having tea at another time would preserve the favorable pairing.

question: A client relies heavily on high-phytate plant staples and wants to improve mineral availability without abandoning them. Which preparation strategy may help?
choices: Soak, sprout, ferment, or cook appropriate foods
Eat every legume and grain completely raw
Add more phytate to bind additional minerals
Remove all sources of iron and zinc
explanation: Phytate can bind minerals such as iron and zinc and reduce their absorption. Preparation processes including soaking, sprouting, fermentation, and cooking can make some of those minerals more available. These methods allow useful plant foods to remain part of the diet.

question: A client obtains omega-3 fat only from flaxseed and assumes the body converts all of its ALA into EPA and DHA. Which correction is appropriate?
choices: Flaxseed contains EPA and DHA exclusively
ALA is not an omega-3 fat
Flaxseed supplies ALA, but conversion to the longer-chain EPA and DHA is limited
The body converts ALA into protein rather than fatty acids
explanation: Flaxseed, chia seed, walnuts, and certain oils provide the short-chain omega-3 fat ALA. The body can convert ALA to EPA and DHA, but that conversion is limited. The forms should therefore not be treated as nutritionally identical.

question: A vegan client eats mostly fries, cookies, and highly processed substitutes and assumes the vegan label guarantees adequacy. What is the strongest improvement?
choices: Build varied meals around legumes, whole grains, vegetables, nuts, and seeds while considering fortification or supplements
Continue unchanged because excluding animal foods supplies every nutrient automatically
Remove legumes and whole grains to reduce variety
Use sweets as the main source of vitamins and minerals
explanation: A nutritionally strong vegan pattern depends on variety and nutrient-rich staples rather than animal-food exclusion alone. Legumes, whole grains, vegetables, nuts, and seeds provide a stronger foundation. Fortified foods or targeted supplements may also be necessary for nutrients that are difficult to obtain.

question: A client adds a heavily marketed superfood while leaving the rest of an unbalanced diet unchanged. What outcome is most realistic?
choices: The single food will compensate for every missing nutrient and habit
The food may contribute nutrients, but overall variety and dietary pattern remain more important
The marketing term guarantees prevention of chronic disease
All other foods become nutritionally unnecessary
explanation: No single food supplies everything the body needs or determines health by itself. A so-called superfood may be nutritious, but it cannot repair an otherwise unbalanced pattern. Variety and the overall diet provide the more meaningful frame.

question: An underweight client wants gradual weight gain but currently skips meals and relies on occasional sweets. Which plan better supports the goal?
choices: Add regular meals with energy-dense nutritious foods, adequate protein, and resistance exercise
Continue skipping meals and eat sweets only once hunger becomes extreme
Eliminate dietary fat because it contains concentrated energy
Avoid resistance exercise so no lean tissue can develop
explanation: Regular meals and nutrient-dense, energy-rich additions can increase intake gradually while supporting overall nutrition. Adequate protein and resistance exercise may help direct some gain toward lean tissue. Sporadic sweets alone do not provide the same nutritional foundation.

question: A client compares intact whole oats with a refined grain product and asks why their nutrient profiles differ. Which structural difference matters most?
choices: Whole grains retain the bran and germ that refining commonly removes
Refined grains retain extra bran and germ not found in whole grains
Refining adds the original fiber-rich outer layers
explanation: Whole grains retain the bran, germ, and endosperm. Processing a grain into a refined product typically strips away the outer bran and the germ, taking fiber and nutrients with them. That structural loss helps explain the resulting nutritional differences.
